parts.visual:
A team builds a beautiful, glowing, 3D button. It looks like a masterpiece of modern art. But when the user tries to buy a shirt, they can't find the button because it was placed at the very bottom of the screen, underneath an ad. The 'Paint' was perfect. The 'Bones' were broken.

The Difference:
1. UX (User Experience): The logic, flow, and psychology of the product. It is the invisible skeleton. UX designers draw black-and-white boxes (Wireframes) to ensure the user can get from A to B without getting angry.
2. UI (User Interface): The visual surface of the product. It is the paint, the typography, the colors, and the micro-animations. UI designers make the experience beautiful and emotionally satisfying.
parts.audio: A beautiful UI cannot save a terrible UX. If the house has a beautiful paint job but the doors open into brick walls, nobody will live there. You must nail the black-and-white wireframes before you ever touch a color palette.

questions.question: What is a 'Wireframe'?
options: A low-fidelity, black-and-white sketch of a screen. It strips away all colors, images, and fonts so the team is forced to only discuss the logical placement of buttons and the flow of information.
questions.correct_answer: A low-fidelity, black-and-white sketch of a screen. It strips away all colors, images, and fonts so the team is forced to only discuss the logical placement of buttons and the flow of information.
questions.explanation: Remove the beauty to test the logic.

questions.question: Listen to the design critique. Why did the UX designer reject the UI designer's new font?
questions.tts_text: The new cursive font looks incredibly elegant. I love the aesthetic. However, our core users are over 60 years old. When we ran the accessibility test, 40% of them couldn't read the cursive font on a mobile screen. We have to change it to Arial.
options: Because Arial is a cursive font.

Accessibility over Aesthetics. A great UI must serve the UX. If a visual choice (like a thin font or low-contrast colors) makes the product physically harder for the target demographic to use, it is objectively bad design, no matter how pretty it is.
Because cursive is for young people.
questions.correct_answer: Accessibility over Aesthetics. A great UI must serve the UX. If a visual choice (like a thin font or low-contrast colors) makes the product physically harder for the target demographic to use, it is objectively bad design, no matter how pretty it is.
questions.explanation: If they can't read it, they won't buy it.

questions.question: Which of these is a pure UX (User Experience) problem, not a UI problem?
options: The red color is too bright.
To delete an account, the user has to click through 7 different confusing menus and re-enter their password three times. The flow is exhausting and creates massive frustration.
questions.correct_answer: To delete an account, the user has to click through 7 different confusing menus and re-enter their password three times. The flow is exhausting and creates massive frustration.
questions.explanation: UX is about friction. UI is about visuals.

questions.question: Why do PMs force designers to create 'Clickable Prototypes' before engineers write code?
options: To test the flow cheaply. A clickable prototype links the wireframes together so it feels like a real app, but it has no actual code behind it. You can put it in front of a user to see if they get confused, saving months of expensive engineering time.
To make the code run faster.
questions.correct_answer: To test the flow cheaply. A clickable prototype links the wireframes together so it feels like a real app, but it has no actual code behind it. You can put it in front of a user to see if they get confused, saving months of expensive engineering time.
questions.explanation: Fake it before you make it.

A black-and-white sketch to focus strictly on layout and logic
